messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 18
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Tax Consultant
  trauma_type: Rape
  pcl5: 74

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Shouting: Shouting, Auditory (Door): Doors opening or slamming, Male Presence: Being alone with men
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
  Memory: Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns

Vignette:
Kwame is an 18-year-old tax consultant who presented for treatment reporting overwhelming anxiety and distress following a sexual assault four months prior. He is a bright and articulate young man, having been fast-tracked into a junior position at a competitive firm, but he now describes his life as having been hollowed out, leaving only fear. The assault occurred at an off-campus party he attended during a visit to a friend's university. He recalls being cornered in a bedroom by another student. The memory of the event is not a continuous narrative for him, but a series of searing, disjointed sensory fragments. He primarily sees it in still frames: the glint of a belt buckle, a spiderweb crack in the ceiling plaster above him, the assailant's face contorted in a silent shout. The shouting itself is a key part of the memory, a torrent of commands that felt like physical blows. He remembers the final, heavy slam of the bedroom door as the man left, and the sharp, metallic taste of blood where his lip had split against his teeth.

In the months since, these fragments have intruded into his daily life with devastating effect. The taste of blood is the most visceral intrusion; he will be eating lunch at his desk and suddenly his own saliva will seem to turn to copper, a phantom taste so vivid it makes him gag. Sometimes, there is no image at all, just a tidal wave of the same helpless terror he felt pinned to the floor, an emotional echo so powerful it leaves him breathless and disoriented in the middle of a client call. At work, the environment has become a minefield. The open-plan office is loud, and any raised voice, even a cheerful shout from across the room, causes him to freeze, his heart hammering against his ribs. The sound of a heavy door slamming shut down the hall is enough to make him jolt, his mind instantly transported back to that bedroom.

His interactions with colleagues have become fraught with a terror he cannot explain to them. He is certain that he is fundamentally unsafe, especially around men. When his manager, a kind man who has been his mentor, calls him into his office for a private consultation and closes the door, Kwame’s body betrays him. His breathing becomes shallow, his palms sweat, and he can’t follow the conversation, his entire being focused on the closed door as a symbol of being trapped. A friendly, unexpected hand on his shoulder from a passing colleague is enough to make him recoil with a gasp, a reaction that has led to more than one awkward apology. He has come to believe that any stranger approaching him is a source of potential harm. Walking from the train station to his office, he finds himself constantly scanning the faces of other pedestrians, his muscles tensed, ready to flinch away from anyone who comes too close.

This pervasive sense of threat has systematically dismantled his life outside of work. He no longer socializes. He has turned down every invitation from friends, especially if it involves going to a bar, a restaurant, or any building he doesn't know. For Kwame, unfamiliar places represent an unacceptable risk; without knowing all the exits and sightlines, he feels utterly exposed, certain that danger is lurking in every blind corner. His world has shrunk to the rigidly controlled and well-worn path between his small apartment and his office building. The isolation is profound. It was after a performance review, where his supervisor gently noted his ‘jumpiness’ and ‘reluctance to engage in one-on-one mentorship,’ that Kwame realized he could not continue this way. The fear of losing the career he had worked so hard for was the one thing that could momentarily override the fear of everything else. He has come to therapy not with a clear sense of hope, but with the desperate, aching need to make his own mind and body feel safe again.
